paras: The threat against a Black rural mail carrier in Lincoln County, Mississippi, was a warning by white residents in January 1903 that a Black man employed to carry mail on a rural route would not be permitted to do the work. The same residents told the federal postal inspector that he would be given "a dose of tar and feathers" if he took the carrier's side. Northern and Southern papers ran the item as one step in a spreading "crusade against negro Federal officeholders" in Mississippi.

According to the dispatch, white people had first served notice on the postmaster at Jackson that Black carriers on the star mail routes must be discontinued. The threat to the inspector invoked Indianola, where he was said to have taken "sides with the negro."

The Lincoln County warning followed the Jackson notice on the day the dispatch was filed, given to the post-office authorities in the county. A Jackson special explained that postal officials had employed a Black man to deliver the mail on a rural route there. White residents then told the inspector that the carrier "will not be permitted to perform the service" and that the inspector himself would be tarred and feathered if he backed the carrier.
None of the reports names the carrier, the inspector, or any of the residents, and none gives a town within the county.
No report of what became of the carrier, of any action by the inspector or the Post Office Department, or of any arrest was found in the coverage.

The story reached the white press as a single special dispatch, dated New Orleans, January 9, in the St. Louis Republic and the Saint Paul Globe, and New Orleans, January 10, "from Jackson, Miss.," in the Alexandria Gazette and the Washington Times. All of these copies appeared on January 10, and the Bryan Morning Eagle in Texas reprinted the item from the Galveston News a week later.

Headlines treated the notice as a political story about officeholding rather than an attack: the Republic used "Crusade Against Negroes," the Globe "Against Negro Officeholders," and the Washington Times "Postal Inspector May Wear Tar and Feathers." The dispatch relayed the residents' terms without comment, and the Gazette and the Globe added that the New Orleans States had warned President Roosevelt that appointing Black men to federal office in the South would lead to bloodshed. No Black-press coverage of the Lincoln County notice was found.

accounts.label: Special dispatch from Jackson via New Orleans
accounts.gist: White people in Lincoln County told the inspector a Black rural carrier would not be permitted to serve and threatened him with tar and feathers if he backed the carrier, following a similar notice at Jackson.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Crusade Against Negroes' (A1), 'Against Negro Officeholders' (A4), 'Postal Inspector May Wear Tar and Feathers' (A3) present the notice as news of a political crusade, without comment.
The Gazette and Globe append the New Orleans States' warning to Roosevelt that Black federal appointments in the South will lead to bloodshed, reported without comment.

versions.value: Dispatch dated New Orleans, Jan. 10 (special from Jackson)

conflicts.note: Same text; the dateline differs by a day. All copies were printed Jan. 10, so a Jan. 9 filing date is more consistent.

record_check.dossier: intimidation: a notice against a Black carrier's employment and a tar-and-feathers threat to the inspector; no one is reported driven out.
threat only; the carrier was barred from the route, not ordered out of the county.
One unnamed Black rural mail carrier (target of the notice); the unnamed postal inspector was threatened.
'The white people' of the county, size and organization not stated; no mob is described.
The Lincoln County job is a rural route (A2, A3); 'star routes' refers to the Jackson notice.

info: The warning was given on the day the dispatch was filed: 'today' in a dispatch dated New Orleans Jan. 9 (A1, A4) or Jan. 10 (A2, A3).
Lincoln County, Mississippi; no town named.
An unnamed Black man employed by postal officials to deliver mail on a rural route in Lincoln County; the unnamed postal inspector was threatened.
'The people' / 'the white people' of Lincoln County; no one named.
No report of the outcome (whether the carrier kept the route, any federal action) was found.
